newsitem.title: USA: Silver purifiers seen as alternative to chlorine.
newsitem.headline: Silver purifiers seen as alternative to chlorine.

text.p: Silver-based water purification systems offer the most reliable and cost-effective alternative to chlorine systems because chlorine is a chemical increasingly coming under fire for the carcinogenic by-products it leaves in water, according to David Eaton, secretary of Institute of Water Ionization Technologies in the U.K. and director of Roseland Hydronics Plc.

"Silver has long been known for its biocidal properties, with one of the earliest recorded examples provided by the ancient Phoenicians who took wine to sea in ships stored in silver urns to preserve the wine," Eaton told the annual conference of U.S. Gold and Silver Institute here.
"There is much other anecdotal evidence including the practice of cowboys in the Old West of putting a silver dollar in their water canteens to preserve the water free from bacteria," he said.
More recently, NASA developed a silver ion generator, the size of a cigar box, weighing six ounces, as a water purifier used in the Apollo space programme in the 1960's, he said.
Progressively restrictive legislation is confronting the use of chemicals, especially chlorine, which for nearly a quarter of a century has been the primary means of water purification.

With increasing pollution, utilities are being forced to put increasing amounts of chlorine into water supplies, but the chemical reaction, that oxidizes impurities when chlorine is added, also forms carcinogenic by-products, he said.
"Silver offers a healthy alternative and the Institute of Water Ionization Technologies has developed silver ion generators for municipal water supplies," Eaton said.
The market for silver ionized swimming pool systems has expanded significantly in the U.S., but in Britain silver ionization has been developed for mainstream drinking water systems.
Silver ion generators are also being used in intensive care and heart transplant units of hospitals, and for use in the poultry processing and brewing industries, he said.

"The sale of silver ionizers is beginning to take off in the U.K. and there are promising growth markets in Scandinavia, Germany and the Far East," Eaton said. "We calculate that requirements for silver globally will increase to about two million ounces annually within five years."

U.S. regulations allow a silver level of 100 parts per billion (ppb) in drinking water, but a silver level of only 20 ppb has been demonstrated to kill the bacteria legionella pneumophilia, the organism that causes Legionnaires disease, he said.
